newsitem.title: UK: UK shut tax loophole due to growing cost - minister.
newsitem.headline: UK shut tax loophole due to growing cost - minister.

text.p: The UK Treasury ended favourable tax treatment for buyback-linked special dividends because of the sharply rising cost to taxpayers, Michael Jack, Financial Secretary to the Treasury, said on Tuesday.
He told Reuters the Treasury had estimated the cost at 680 million stg minimum in the current and next two financial years.

Jack, who is attending the Conservative party's annual conference, said the Treasury had considered changing the tax treatment at the time of the last finance bill, which implemented last November's budget.

"Then the number of people using this scheme was very much at the level of the trickle, but the trickle has turned into something of a river," Jack said. "We felt the time had now come to stop this particular river because it was getting very expensive for the taxpayer."

Jack stressed that companies could continue to buy back their share capital through stock market transactions. "On-market share buy-backs aren't affected by these proposals because that's a straightforward return of capital to the shareholders and doesn't require any of the inventive mechanisms that have been created to channel these funds to exempt institutions."
Jack said Reuters Holdings Plc had been even more creative by designing its scheme in a way that benefited individual shareholders.

He was speaking after a statement by Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke removing some of the tax advantages which had applied to pension funds, which are exempt from tax and which had been able to reclaim the 25 percent advance corporation tax paid by companies on dividends.
Clarke said pension funds could no longer claim tax credits -- which mean that a one stg net dividend is worth 1.25 stg to a pension fund -- on buy-backs or on some special dividends.
The new rules apply immediately to any company repurchasing its shares or making special payouts associated with a share consolidation or a takeover.

"The share buy-back arrangements which are effectively special dividends have been the subject of increasing usage (and) end up... with the net result that the exempt institution gains, the company gains and the taxpayer foots the bill.

"There does come a time when you can see the bill growing, and you have to draw a line," he said. "There have been quite a lot, and I think our sense is that there were a lot waiting in the wings...The cost of it was rising to an unacceptable level."
